So the 98.1% / 98.2% numbers are obtained by two software pipelines on top of the same FPA, not by running the fabricated MCA against a fabricated SCA. The abstract and introduction phrasing leads readers to infer a hardware demonstration that did not happen, and any claim of 'faster training' carries the same caveat. This needs explicit acknowledgement in the abstract, results, and conclusions.

Comparison between MCA and SCA does not control for input-dimensionality, confounding 'spectral channels' with 'wider classifier input': MCA feeds a 6-channel-per-pixel tensor into the classifier; SCA feeds 1 channel per pixel. The classifier therefore sees 6x more features per spatial location with MCA, which alone explains faster convergence and higher small-sample accuracy even if every MCA channel were spectrally redundant. The standard control — replicating the SCA channel six times, or projecting MCA back to a single channel by averaging — is not run. Without this control, the gap (e.g., 33 pp at 10 epochs, 5 pp at 100 epochs) cannot be attributed to genuine spectral diversity. This confound undermines the central claim that the device's 'parallel processing' is what improves recognition, and it contaminates every numerical comparison in Fig 4 and the conclusions.

Imaging / simulation pipeline is described in two sentences; classifier architecture, dataset size, splits, and forward model are absent: The strongest application claim depends entirely on the imaging simulation, yet the main text gives no information about: (i) the classifier (architecture, depth, loss, optimizer, regularization, learning rate); (ii) the dataset (number of gesture images per class, number of curled-finger images, total size, class balance, subject hold-out); (iii) the train/val/test split; (iv) the forward model that converts a Melexis frame into per-channel MCA outputs (which channel-response curves are used? do they include device-to-device variability or only the average curve?); and (v) the OPENZYNQ commit / configuration. Combined with the missing dataset and code (see the data-availability comment), the 98.1% / 98.2% numbers are not independently reproducible.

Detection-band claim ('IR-C band, 3 microns to 1 mm') overstates the demonstrated operating window; biological-thermal claim has no passive measurement: Two compounding problems. (1) The phrase 'detection range within the IR-C band (3 μm to 1 mm)' is technically true (the operating window is a subset of IR-C), but reads as if the device covers the full band. The device's measured plasmon resonance peaks span ~1084-1292 cm^-1, i.e. ~7.7-9.2 microns; the laser used (Methods 'Measurements') tunes only 2.3-10 microns. (2) The text immediately leverages this to claim relevance to human thermal radiation in 8-14 microns, but no passive measurement (e.g., a warm body in front of the device with no laser) is reported; the photocurrent characterization always uses an active laser source < 1 mW. The pivot from 'this band overlaps biological thermal radiation' to 'our device can handle it' is therefore an inferential leap unsupported by the experiments shown.

'Epoch' is defined inconsistently: results paragraph says 3,600 iterations, Fig 4 captions say 1,000: The body of Section 'Multichannel infrared imaging' says each epoch is 3,600 iterations (and that gesture training reached its plateau 'after 3,600 iterations'). Fig 4 captions, however, state '100 epochs ... with each epoch consisting of 1,000 iterations' for both the gesture experiment (b, c) and the curled-finger experiment (d, e). Total training compute therefore differs by a factor of 3.6 depending on which definition is used, and the 'faster training speed' claim is unanchored. Either the body or the captions must be corrected.

Asymmetric contact-metal scheme is named inconsistently (Pd/Ti vs Au/Ti and Au/Ni) and the metals determine the zero-bias claim: Section 'Type-printing' says the asymmetric contacts are 20 nm Pd and 20 nm Ti capped with 80 nm Au. Methods 'Device fabrication' instead names 'Au/Ti and Au/Ni' as the source and drain in one sentence, then names 'Ti and Pd layers' in the very next sentence — three different metals (Ti, Ni, Pd) within one paragraph. The work-function asymmetry between source and drain is the physical origin of the zero-bias photocurrent, so the choice (Pd/Ti ~5.2/4.3 eV vs Ti/Ni ~4.3/5.0 eV) materially affects the central claim. The reader cannot determine which configuration was actually fabricated and characterized.

Stripe geometry: W (period), w (single-domain width), and d (in eqn 1) are used interchangeably across sections: Section 'Type-printing' defines W = period (200 nm-1 μm) and w = single-domain width (100-500 nm), with W = 2w. Eqn (1) uses a third variable d for 'ferroelectric superdomain width'. Fig 3a and Section 'Multichannel infrared imaging' both refer to 'a ferroelectric domain width' ranging '100 to 500 nm' for the MCA and 500 nm for the SCA — values that match w, not W. Because eqn (1) uses q ~ N pi/d, whether d is the period or the single-domain width changes predicted plasmon frequencies by a factor of ~2. The notation must be reconciled across the paper.

POG-to-E_F conversion (mu_c = +121 meV upward, -448 meV downward) is asserted with no value of alpha' or pristine baseline: These chemical potentials drive the FEM simulation in Fig 2j-k and the predicted spectrum from eqn (1). They are derived from POG values 1586 cm^-1 (upward) and 1597 cm^-1 (downward), an 11 cm^-1 splitting. Converting that to E_F requires the integral constant alpha'; ref 29 gives a specific numerical value but the paper neither states alpha' nor identifies the pristine-graphene reference POG. The asymmetry |+121|:|-448| ~ 1:3.7 implies a substantial baseline shift between 'upward' and 'pristine' graphene, but that baseline is never stated in the main text. Without alpha' and the reference POG, the chemical potentials — and the simulation built on them — cannot be reproduced.

Photoresponsivity '~30 mA/W' is reported without wavelength, illumination intensity, device area, or per-cell breakdown: Responsivity for graphene plasmonic detectors depends sensitively on wavelength, illumination intensity (laser spot vs uniform flood), device active area, and operating temperature. The text reports a single rounded value, doesn't say which of the six MCA cells produced it, doesn't give the spot size (only that laser power < 1 mW), and doesn't normalize for area. Comparison plots in Fig 3e against refs 31-34 — including waveguide-integrated graphene detectors with multi-A/W responsivities — therefore cannot be evaluated for fairness. The conclusions section then drops the 'comparable, not highest' qualifier and calls 30 mA/W 'high', which compounds the issue.

Number of usable spectral channels is unclear; six cells share only ~200 cm^-1 of tuning with no FWHM or cross-talk reported: The MCA pixel is described as 6-channel, but six resonance peaks span only 1084-1292 cm^-1 (~16% relative tuning). Typical graphene plasmonic linewidths in this regime are 50-100 cm^-1 (refs 13, 15), so adjacent peaks likely overlap heavily. The paper reports neither per-channel FWHM nor a measured cross-talk matrix. Because the 'six channels per pixel' framing supports the claim of replacing multi-grating / multi-camera systems, the practical channel count needs explicit characterization.

Numerical-simulations Methods paragraph defers all configuration details (RPA gamma, FEM mesh, BFO eps_r, OPENZYNQ classifier) to the supplement: Three different simulation chains are central to the paper's results. The Methods main-text covers them in three sentences and refers all parameters to supplementary sections: RPA scattering rate / temperature / Fermi velocity, FEM mesh resolution, BFO permittivity (eps_r), substrate boundary conditions, OPENZYNQ classifier architecture and training hyperparameters. Even acknowledging that supplements exist, key parameters that materially shift omega_spr (eps_r, gamma) and the test accuracies (classifier choice) belong in the main text given how prominently the simulation results are featured.

Dataset, code, and trained-model availability is too thin to support reproducibility of ML claims: The paper points to a public OPENZYNQ repo for the simulation framework but does not link a specific commit, the gesture/curled-finger image dataset, the trained-model weights, or the training scripts. A 'Nature Communications'-class paper that reports headline ML accuracies (98.1% / 98.2%) and uses those numbers in the abstract should make the dataset and pipeline available. As described, the central application result cannot be independently reproduced.

Photocurrent measurements 'averaged from 12 points' with no error bars or device-to-device statistics: Twelve sample points per wavelength are averaged, but neither standard deviation nor inter-device reproducibility is reported. Given that the fabrication relies on AFM-tip-written stripes from 100 nm-1 μm, stripe-width variability and ferroelectric-polarization inhomogeneity are obvious reproducibility threats. Without error bars on Fig 3d, claims of 'remarkably selective' resonance and 'enhanced' photoresponsivity rest on a single curve per cell.

Selective detection factor beta is defined but never reported numerically: Beta is presented as the figure of merit for spectral selectivity but no per-cell numerical value is given. Since spectral selectivity is the main differentiator versus broadband detectors (refs 30-34), an explicit beta per cell is the natural way to support the 'selective' framing and the 6-channel claim. Currently it is asserted qualitatively from Fig 3d.

Edge-detection 'gesture' and 'curled-finger' datasets: size, class balance, source, and split unspecified: The number of training images per class, total dataset size, train/val/test split, and whether subjects/scenes were held out are not stated. Image collection method ('Melexis 192x144 IR camera') is described only at the system level. Standard ML reporting requires these basic statistics; without them it is impossible to judge whether 98.1% / 98.2% indicate genuine generalization or memorization of a small dataset.

AFM type-printing throughput, yield, and write-time over 5 mm x 5 mm / 10 mm x 10 mm samples are not reported: AFM-tip writing of 100 nm stripes over the 5 mm x 5 mm or 10 mm x 10 mm samples described in Section 'Rescaling' is, in principle, an extremely slow serial process. The paper alludes to a 'water-printing' alternative (ref 27, Tian 2018) without saying which technique was used for which device, what the per-mm^2 write time is, or how stripe uniformity was verified. Because 'printable' / 'simple fabrication' is a headline benefit, this is a methodology gap that bears directly on the central scalability claim.
